glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: Proverbs 17 prizes a quiet home above a feasting one and sets every heart before the LORD who tests it, then shows how covered offenses, early peacemaking, honest judgment, and few words hold households and friendships together while the fool and the bribe pull them apart.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: The chapter sits within 16:1–22:16, where Solomon’s sayings unfold under the LORD who directs human steps. Its single sayings gather around the home, friendship, the courts, and the fool.

glance.label: Chapter Outline

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “The refining pot is for silver and the furnace for gold, But the LORD tests the hearts.” (Proverbs 17:3)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
Proverbs 17 begins at the table: “Better is a dry morsel with quietness, Than a house full of feasting with strife” (17:1). The household keeps returning. A wise servant can rise above a son who brings shame (17:2), grandchildren crown the old (17:6), and a foolish son is “bitterness to her who bore him” (17:25). Near the opening stands the chapter’s word about God. Silver goes into the refining pot and gold into the furnace, “But the LORD tests the hearts” (17:3). Fire brings out what is really in the metal and burns away the dross, and the LORD does the same with the inner life that a full table or a family name can hide.

From the heart the sayings move to what passes between people. Love covers an offense, while repeating it “separates friends” (17:9). A quarrel starts like water through a breach, so wisdom stops it early (17:14). “A friend loves at all times” (17:17), yet the very next saying refuses a rash pledge for that friend (17:18). The courts come into view as well, where a bribe slipped “behind the back” bends justice (17:23). Through it all walks the fool, more dangerous than a bear robbed of her cubs (17:12), until the chapter closes on the wisdom of a shut mouth (17:28).

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Proverbs 17:1–6 — Quiet Homes and Tested Hearts

A crust eaten in peace outranks a feast full of quarrels, and a wise servant can come to share the inheritance of a son who brings shame. At the center the LORD tests hearts as fire proves silver and gold, exposing those who relish slander or mock the poor, while honor passes both ways between grandparents, parents, and children.

Proverbs 17:7–13 — Rebuke, Love That Covers, and the Fool’s Folly

Fine speech sits badly on a fool and lies far worse on a ruler, and a gift looks like a lucky charm to the one who hands it out. Love covers an offense while retelling it divides friends, one rebuke reaches a wise man deeper than a hundred blows reach a fool, and the rebel, the fool caught up in his folly, and the man who repays good with evil all bring on trouble that will not stay away.

Proverbs 17:14–20 — Strife, Justice, and the Faithful Friend

Strife is framed at both ends of this cluster: a quarrel should be stopped at the first trickle, and the one who loves strife loves transgression and builds his own gate high. Between them the LORD detests twisted verdicts in either direction, the fool tries to buy wisdom he has no heart for, and a friend’s steady love is kept wise by refusing rash pledges for that friend’s debt.

Proverbs 17:21–28 — A Merry Heart and Restrained Words

A foolish son brings sorrow to his father and bitterness to his mother, a grief the sayings voice without assigning blame, while a merry heart does the whole person good and a broken spirit dries the bones. The section condemns the hidden bribe and the punishing of the upright, sets wisdom right before the eyes of the discerning while the fool gazes at the ends of the earth, and closes by praising sparing words and a calm spirit.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Proverbs 17 shows that the LORD cares about the air a family breathes. Peace around a plain meal is the better portion (17:1), and the sayings on covering offenses and stopping quarrels early (17:9, 14) give households and friends a way to keep it. The chapter also speaks honestly about the grief of a fool’s parents (17:21, 25) without making them the cause of his folly.

The verdict of 17:15 bears on the gospel. Because the LORD detests anyone who “justifies the wicked,” His justifying “the ungodly” (Romans 4:5) cannot mean that He overlooks guilt. Paul shows that God does it through faith in Jesus, so that He remains “just and the justifier” (Romans 3:26). Mercy in Christ never bends justice; it is grounded in the cross, where justice was satisfied.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
The LORD who tests hearts. As fire proves silver and gold, the LORD brings out what is in a person and refines it; His testing reveals and purifies, and not every trial is punishment for sin (17:3).

Peace and honor at home. Quiet is worth more than plenty, generations honor one another, and a fool’s folly wounds both father and mother (17:1–2, 6, 13, 21, 25).

Covering, quarreling, and faithful friends. Love lets an offense go, strife is stopped before it spreads, and loyal friendship stays steady in adversity while still refusing rash pledges (17:9, 14, 17–19).

Justice that cannot be bought. The chapter notices how people trust in gifts and then condemns the secret bribe, the unjust verdict, and the punishing of the upright (17:8, 15, 23, 26).

Restrained words and a calm spirit. Lying lips, a perverse tongue, and spiteful talk bring trouble, while the man of knowledge spares his words and keeps a cool temper (17:4, 7, 20, 27–28).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
Tests the hearts (17:3). The picture comes from the refiner’s work. Heat shows whether metal is genuine and separates it from what is worthless, and the LORD’s examination of the inner person does both.

Covers a transgression (17:9). To forgive a personal wrong and refuse to spread it, as “love covers all sins” (10:12). It never means hiding abuse or crime.

A present and a bribe (17:8, 23). Verse 8 describes how a gift looks to the one who gives it, like a precious stone that seems to open every door. Verse 23 names the bribe taken in secret “To pervert the ways of justice,” and the Law warns that “a bribe blinds the discerning” (Exodus 23:8).

Surety (17:18). Shaking hands to guarantee another person’s debt. Proverbs warns against it repeatedly as rash, without forbidding all help to a friend (compare 6:1–5).

The fool (17:10, 12, 16, 24). A person whose trouble is moral, not mental: he refuses correction, acts out his folly, and lets his eyes wander from wisdom that is right in front of him. These sayings are never a slur on people of limited ability.

A merry heart (17:22). Joy reaches the body as well as the soul, and a crushed spirit wears it down. The saying offers no rebuke to the sick or depressed and no substitute for medical care.

focus: Proverbs 17 gathers sayings on peace in the household and the LORD who tests hearts, the fool and the value of rebuke, strife and the faithful friend, and the quiet speech that marks understanding.

sections.title: Quiet Homes and Tested Hearts
sections.summary: A dry morsel with quietness is better than a house of feasting with strife. The LORD tests the hearts, whoever mocks the poor reproaches his Maker, and grandchildren are the crown of the old.

sections.title: Rebuke, Love That Covers, and the Fool’s Folly
sections.summary: He who covers a transgression seeks love, but repeating a matter separates friends. Rebuke reaches the wise more than a hundred blows reach a fool, and it is safer to meet a bear robbed of her cubs than a fool in his folly.

sections.title: Strife, Justice, and the Faithful Friend
sections.summary: Strife begins like releasing water, so it should be stopped early. Justifying the wicked and condemning the just are both an abomination to the LORD, and a friend loves at all times while a brother is born for adversity.

sections.title: A Merry Heart and Restrained Words
sections.summary: A foolish son grieves his parents, while a merry heart does good like medicine. A bribe perverts justice, and he who has knowledge spares his words; even a fool is counted wise when he holds his peace.

1.brief: A plain, dry meal eaten in peace is better than a house full of feasting where people quarrel. The chapter opens by setting quietness above abundance, since plenty cannot make up for a home torn by strife.
1.explain:
“Better is a dry morsel with quietness,”

A “dry morsel” is a crust of bread with nothing to soften it: no oil, no wine, no stew to dip it in. It is the plain fare of a poor or simple table. Yet the saying sets it beside “quietness,” the settled ease of a home where no one is bracing for the next argument. The bread is not praised for being dry, and poverty is not held up as a virtue. What gives this meal its worth is the peace around it.

“Than a house full of feasting with strife.”

The other house has everything a table could hold. The word behind “feasting” is the ordinary Hebrew word for sacrifices, which points to the meat of offerings that a worshiper and his household shared at a celebration meal. Such a house might look both prosperous and devout. Then the line ends on the two words that undo it all: “with strife.” Quarreling spoils the abundance, and even a religious feast is no compensation for a home at war with itself. Proverbs has weighed peace against plenty before, but this opening saying adds that outward devotion cannot make up for strife either. The chapter will come back to strife in 17:14 and 17:19.
1.notes:
The Hebrew word translated “feasting” is zebach, the ordinary word for a sacrifice, especially the kind of sacrifice whose meat was eaten at a feast. The KJV keeps the literal word “sacrifices” in its text, with a margin reading “good cheer.” Most modern versions, like the NKJV, render the word “feasting,” since a sacrificial meal was the great feast of an ordinary household. The law describes the worshiper eating the meat of his peace offering: “The flesh of the sacrifice of his peace offering for thanksgiving shall be eaten the same day it is offered” (Leviticus 7:15).

Two earlier “better” sayings make a similar comparison: “Better is a little with the fear of the LORD, Than great treasure with trouble” (15:16) and “Better is a dinner of herbs where love is, Than a fatted calf with hatred” (15:17).

2.brief: Character can overturn the expected order in a household: a wise servant may come to rule over a son who brings shame, and even share the inheritance with the brothers. Birth does not guarantee a son’s place, and faithful wisdom can win what shameful conduct throws away.
2.explain:
“A wise servant will rule over a son who causes shame,”

In an Israelite household the son was the heir and the servant worked under the family, so the expected order placed the son above the servant. This saying reverses that order. The servant is “wise,” prudent and capable in the way he handles affairs, while the son is one “who causes shame,” disgracing his family by the way he lives. Over time the faithful servant can come to manage the household and even hold authority over the son who has wasted his position.

“And will share an inheritance among the brothers.”

The second line goes further. The servant not only rules; he receives a portion of the family estate as though he were one of the brothers. Scripture shows that such a thing could happen. Before Isaac was born, Abram expected his property to pass to a servant: “the heir of my house is Eliezer of Damascus” (Genesis 15:2). The proverb is not a rule of inheritance law, and it does not promise that every faithful servant will be rewarded this way. It observes that birth gives a person a place, but character determines whether he keeps it. A son can throw away by shameful living what a servant gains by wise and faithful service.
2.notes: The phrase “a son who causes shame” also describes the lazy son of harvest time: “He who sleeps in harvest is a son who causes shame” (10:5). A similar phrase describes the son who mistreats his parents in 19:26.

3.brief: Silver is proved in the refining pot and gold in the furnace, and in the same way the LORD tests human hearts. Only He can examine the inner person, and His testing brings out what is really there and purifies it, as fire does with precious metal.
3.explain:
“The refining pot is for silver and the furnace for gold,”

The first line comes from a metalworker’s shop. Silver was heated in a refining pot, or crucible, and gold in a furnace. The heat did two things at once: it separated the dross from the metal, and it proved whether the metal was genuine. The metals in view are silver and gold, precious materials worth the refiner’s effort.

“But the LORD tests the hearts.”

The word “But” turns from the workshop to God. What fire does for metal, the LORD does for “the hearts,” the inner person with its thoughts, motives, and desires. Human refiners can test silver and gold, but no human tool can reach a heart. Only the LORD can examine it, and He does. His testing brings out what is really there, and it purifies, as the refiner’s fire does. The picture is of a refiner who values what he works with and tests it to prove and purify it. Not every hardship a person faces is God testing him for sin; the verse speaks of God’s searching knowledge and refining work. Set near the start of a chapter about households, friendships, and courts, the saying places every relationship that follows under the eyes of the LORD who sees the heart.
3.notes:
The first line is repeated word for word at 27:21, where it is completed differently: “And a man is valued by what others say of him” (27:21). There praise becomes the test that reveals a person.

The Hebrew verb behind “tests” is bachan, which means to examine something closely in order to prove what it really is. It is used elsewhere for God’s examination of people, as in “For the righteous God tests the hearts and minds” (Psalm 7:9). Here the word links the refiner’s fire in the first line with God’s searching of the heart in the second. The image differs from 16:2, where the LORD “weighs the spirits” as on a scale; here He tests them as with fire.

4.brief: People are drawn to words that match their own hearts: the evildoer pays attention to false lips, and the liar listens eagerly to a spiteful tongue. What a person enjoys hearing exposes what he is, so a taste for slander is itself a mark of wickedness.
4.explain:
“An evildoer gives heed to false lips;”

Proverbs often warns against the person who speaks lies. This saying turns to the person who listens. An “evildoer” is someone who habitually does wrong, and he “gives heed” to “false lips,” paying close attention to deceptive talk. He listens because the lies serve him. They confirm his suspicions, feed his schemes, or excuse his own conduct. Falsehood needs an audience to spread, and he supplies one.

“A liar listens eagerly to a spiteful tongue.”

The second line sharpens the first. The listener is now called “a liar,” and he “listens eagerly,” leaning in to catch every word of “a spiteful tongue,” speech meant to wound and ruin. The pairing is deliberate. A man who deals in lies enjoys hearing malicious words because they match his own heart. What a person loves to hear reveals what he is. The verse makes the listener responsible as well as the speaker, and it exposes the appetite that keeps slander moving from mouth to ear. The LORD who tests the hearts in 17:3 sees not only what people say but what they are eager to hear.

5.brief: Mocking the poor is an insult aimed at God, because the poor man bears the work of his Maker (compare 14:31). The second line widens the warning to anyone who is glad when disaster strikes another; that kind of cruelty will not go unpunished.
5.explain:
“He who mocks the poor reproaches his Maker;”

To “mock” the poor is to laugh at them, ridicule their condition, or treat them with contempt. The saying declares that this “reproaches his Maker.” It insults the God who made that poor person. The LORD made rich and poor alike, as Proverbs says elsewhere: “The LORD is the maker of them all” (22:2). Contempt for the poor therefore lands on Him. An earlier saying spoke of the one who “oppresses” the poor (14:31); this one shows that no money or rights need be taken. Ridicule alone is enough to insult God.

“He who is glad at calamity will not go unpunished.”

The second line moves from contempt to gloating. “Calamity” is disaster, the day ruin falls on someone. A person can be “glad” about it without saying a word, quietly pleased when a rival or an unfortunate neighbor suffers. The verse declares that such a person “will not go unpunished,” which implies that God takes notice and will hold him to account. The two lines describe the same kind of heart, one that lifts itself by looking down on others, first on their poverty and then on their pain. The God who tests hearts sees the secret gladness as clearly as the open sneer.
5.notes: Proverbs gives a direct command on the same subject: “Do not rejoice when your enemy falls, And do not let your heart be glad when he stumbles” (24:17).

6.brief: Grandchildren are a crown that honors the old, and children find their glory in their father. The saying pictures a family in which honor flows both ways across the generations, each giving the other something to be proud of.
6.explain:
“Children’s children are the crown of old men,”

A “crown” is a mark of honor worn where everyone can see it. For the old, grandchildren are that crown. In Israel, living to see a third generation was counted a blessing from God; Psalm 128 closes with the wish, “Yes, may you see your children’s children” (Psalm 128:6). A growing family meant that a man’s name and household would continue after him. The line assumes a family in which the younger generation brings credit to the older.

“And the glory of children is their father.”

The second line runs in the other direction. Children take pride in their father. His name, character, and reputation are their “glory,” something they can hold their heads up about. Together the two lines picture honor flowing both down and up the generations, each giving the other reason to be glad. The second line also carries a quiet expectation: a father ought to live in a way his children are glad to claim. That prepares for the later sayings in this chapter, at 17:21 and 17:25, where a foolish son brings his parents sorrow instead of joy. The proverb describes God’s good design for families. It does not measure the worth of those who have no grandchildren or whose fathers gave them little to be proud of.

7.brief: Fine, noble speech does not suit a fool, and lying lips suit a ruler far less. The argument moves from the lesser to the greater: if eloquence seems out of place in a fool’s mouth, falsehood is even more out of place in one entrusted with leading others.
7.explain:
“Excellent speech is not becoming to a fool,”

“Excellent speech” is lofty, polished language, the kind of words that belong to a person of dignity. “Becoming” means fitting or suitable. Fine words in a fool’s mouth sound hollow because his life contradicts them. The fool in this verse is the coarse, godless kind, the man who has no regard for God or for others, and noble words from his mouth are contradicted by the way he lives.

“Much less lying lips to a prince.”

“Much less” signals an argument from the lesser to the greater. If eloquence is out of place in a fool, lying is far more out of place in a “prince,” a nobleman or ruler entrusted with leadership and judgment. People depend on a ruler’s word, so when he lies, the harm reaches everyone under his authority. The saying ties speech to character and calling: words should fit the person, and the higher a person’s responsibility, the more a lie betrays it. The chapter uses the same word for nobles again at 17:26, where upright princes are wrongly punished.
7.notes:
The Hebrew word for “fool” here is nabal. It describes a person who is senseless toward God and coarse toward others, and it is the name of the man of whom Abigail said, “Nabal is his name, and folly is with him!” (1 Samuel 25:25). The Hebrew word for “prince” is nadib, which describes a person who is noble in rank and also noble and generous in character. Isaiah sets the same two words side by side: “The foolish person will no longer be called generous” (Isaiah 32:5). The pairing helps explain the verse: the nabal and the nadib are opposites in character as well as in station.

The KJV margin gives the literal Hebrew behind “excellent speech” as ‘a lip of excellency,’ that is, speech of abundance or superiority. Most versions take it as fine or eloquent speech, while the 1984 NIV reads “Arrogant lips,” understanding the excess as pride.

8.brief: Here a gift or bribe is seen through the eyes of the one who uses it: to him it is like a precious stone, a charm that seems to open every door. The proverb observes how people trust in gifts to get their way; it does not approve bribery, which verse 23 plainly condemns.
8.explain:
“A present is a precious stone in the eyes of its possessor;”

The Hebrew word translated “present” is the same word rendered “bribe” in 17:23. The word by itself names a gift given to gain something, but here the setting shows what kind of gift is meant: a payment used to buy influence, as 17:23 makes plain. The key phrase is “in the eyes of its possessor.” The verse reports how the gift looks to the person who holds it and hands it out. To him it is “a precious stone,” a gem or charm that seems to carry good fortune with it. He trusts his gift the way someone else might trust a lucky stone.

“Wherever he turns, he prospers.”

From his point of view, it works. Every door he approaches seems to open, and every official he pays seems to cooperate. Proverbs is honest that corrupt methods often appear to succeed for a time. Yet the verse describes how a briber sees things; it does not approve of what he does. The same Hebrew word returns in 17:23, where the chapter names the bribe plainly and states its purpose: “To pervert the ways of justice.” Read together, the two sayings give both sides, the briber’s confidence and the damage his payment does. A gift freely given in generosity is a different matter, and Proverbs can speak of it without condemnation: “A man’s gift makes room for him” (18:16).
8.notes:
Both “present” here and “bribe” in 17:23 translate the Hebrew word shochad, a gift or payment given to win someone’s favor. Most often it names a bribe, as in “you shall take no bribe” (Exodus 23:8). In 6:35, though, the same word describes gifts offered to a wronged husband: “Nor will he be appeased though you give many gifts” (6:35). The setting, not the word alone, shows when a corrupt payment is meant. In this chapter, 17:23 makes the corrupt purpose clear.

The Hebrew behind “precious stone” is literally ‘a stone of favor,’ and the KJV margin renders it ‘a stone of grace.’ Many interpreters understand it as a charm or lucky stone believed to bring good fortune, and the NASB and the 1984 NIV render it “a charm.” That reading suits the verse, since the briber expects his gift to win favor wherever he goes.

9.brief: Love looks for ways to cover an offense, forgiving it and not spreading it, and so it keeps friendship whole. The one who keeps bringing the matter up, repeating it to others or raising it again, drives close friends apart (compare 10:12); covering a personal wrong is not the same as hiding abuse or crime.
9.explain:
“He who covers a transgression seeks love,”

A “transgression” is an offense, a wrong done against someone. To “cover” it is to let it rest: to forgive it, to refuse to broadcast it, and to stop holding it over the offender. The verb “seeks” shows that covering is active. The one who covers is going after love, valuing the friendship more than winning the point. Proverbs has already said that “love covers all sins” (10:12); this saying shows covering as the way love pursues and keeps a relationship. Covering a personal wrong in this sense never means concealing abuse or crime, hiding danger from those who need protection, or shielding wrongdoing from proper authority. The verse speaks of offenses between friends, and it gives no cover to an abuser.

“But he who repeats a matter separates friends.”

To “repeat” a matter can mean two things. A person may repeat it to others, spreading the story until everyone knows. Or he may keep bringing it up with the friend himself, refusing to let it rest. Either way the result is the same: he “separates friends.” The whisperer of chapter 16 does the same damage, for he “separates the best of friends” (16:28). Repeating an offense, whether to others or to the friend himself, keeps the wound open and can drive even close friends apart.
9.notes: The Hebrew verb behind “repeats” means to do or say something a second time, which allows both senses: telling the matter to others and raising it again with the offender.

10.brief: One rebuke goes deeper into a wise man than a hundred blows into a fool. The wise person takes correction to heart, while the fool, whose problem is moral and not mental, can be beaten again and again and still refuse to learn.
10.explain:
“Rebuke is more effective for a wise man”

A “rebuke” is a word of correction, telling someone plainly that he is wrong. “More effective” translates a Hebrew verb that means to go down or sink in; the rebuke goes deep into a wise man. The wise person is not someone who never needs correction. He is someone a word can reach. He hears the rebuke, takes it to heart, and changes.

“Than a hundred blows on a fool.”

“A hundred blows” is deliberate exaggeration. A fool can be beaten again and again and still learn nothing. The difference lies in the heart that receives the correction, not in its strength. The fool’s problem is moral, not mental: he refuses instruction, so neither words nor force get through to him. The verse does not commend harsh treatment. It measures the distance between a teachable heart, which one word can turn, and a hardened one that a hundred blows cannot.
10.notes: The law of Moses limited a court-ordered beating: “Forty blows he may give him and no more” (Deuteronomy 25:3). A hundred blows is far beyond any lawful punishment, which marks the number as hyperbole.

11.brief: Bent on evil, a man looks for nothing but rebellion, and so a cruel messenger will be sent against him. The one who rises against rightful authority will eventually meet stern judgment, pictured as a harsh officer sent to deal with the rebel.
11.explain:
“An evil man seeks only rebellion;”

The evil man here has one aim. “Seeks only” describes a settled direction of life, not a single misstep. His goal is “rebellion,” defiance of rightful authority. Placed right after the saying about the wise man whom a rebuke can reach, this man is the opposite: he has refused correction and set himself against those placed over him.

“Therefore a cruel messenger will be sent against him.”

“Therefore” ties the consequence to the cause. Because he pursues rebellion, “a cruel messenger will be sent against him.” In the setting of a kingdom, this pictures an officer dispatched by the king to deal with a rebel, harsh and unsparing in carrying out his task. The words “will be sent” do not say who sends him, but they make clear that someone with authority acts. Behind every rightful authority stands the LORD who judges, and the man who keeps choosing rebellion will finally meet a severity he has brought on himself. The verse states a general truth about settled defiance; it does not mean that every hardship is a sign of rebellion.
11.notes:
The Hebrew word for “messenger” is the ordinary word for a messenger and also the word used for angels. Some readers hear an angel of judgment here, but a royal officer fits the immediate picture, as in “As messengers of death is the king’s wrath” (16:14).

The Hebrew of the first line can be read with either word as the subject. The NKJV, ESV and KJV read the evil man seeking rebellion, while the NASB and AMP read ‘A rebellious man seeks only evil.’ The sense is close either way.

12.brief: It would be safer to run into a mother bear robbed of her cubs than to meet a fool in the middle of his folly. The startling picture warns that a fool acting out his folly is more dangerous and less predictable than an enraged animal.
12.explain:
“Let a man meet a bear robbed of her cubs,”

A mother bear robbed of her cubs was a familiar picture of savage fury in Israel. Bears lived in the land, and shepherds knew the danger; David told Saul of the time “when a lion or a bear came and took a lamb out of the flock” (1 Samuel 17:34). Hushai described David’s men as enraged “like a bear robbed of her cubs in the field” (2 Samuel 17:8). The saying says it would be better to run into such an animal.

“Rather than a fool in his folly.”

The comparison is startling on purpose. A fool “in his folly,” caught up in the full flow of his foolishness, is more dangerous than an enraged bear. The bear’s fury is terrible, yet the verse ranks the fool as the greater danger. The fool acting out his folly listens to no reason, and the damage he does can spread through a household, a business, or a community. The verse also implies the wise course: some meetings should be avoided, and wisdom recognizes when to stay out of a fool’s path. As elsewhere in Proverbs, the “fool” is someone who morally refuses wisdom, and the saying is no insult to people of limited ability.
12.notes: The LORD uses the same image of His own judgment on Israel: “I will meet them like a bear deprived of her cubs” (Hosea 13:8). In the NKJV both verses use the verb “meet.”

13.brief: Whoever repays good with evil brings lasting trouble on his own household, for evil will not leave his house. Ingratitude of this kind invites harm that stays, reaching beyond the man himself to the people who live under his roof.
13.explain:
“Whoever rewards evil for good,”

To “reward” here is to repay. This man answers kindness with harm. Someone treated him well, helped him, or trusted him, and he paid that goodness back with injury. Repaying evil for evil is sin; repaying evil for good is worse, because it turns another person’s kindness into the occasion for hurting him. It is ingratitude in its ugliest form.

“Evil will not depart from his house.”

The consequence reaches beyond the man to his “house,” his household and family. The evil he sent out comes back and settles in. David’s life shows the pattern. He repaid the loyal Uriah with adultery and murder, and the LORD told him, “the sword shall never depart from your house” (2 Samuel 12:10). That account illustrates what the verse states as a general rule. Like other proverbs, this one describes how God’s ordered world tends to work. It does not explain every trouble that comes to a family, and it gives no one the right to trace a household’s suffering to a hidden sin.
13.notes: The psalmist uses the same expression of his enemies: “They reward me evil for good, To the sorrow of my soul” (Psalm 35:12).

14.brief: Starting a quarrel is like opening a small breach in a dam: once the water begins to flow, it widens and is hard to stop. So the wise course is to drop the matter before the quarrel breaks out, because strife is far easier to prevent than to contain.
14.explain:
“The beginning of strife is like releasing water;”

The picture is of water held back by a dam or stored in a cistern. Open a small breach and the water begins to trickle out; then the flow wears the opening wider until it cannot be stopped. A quarrel works the same way. The first sharp word or the first refusal to let something pass seems small, yet once strife begins, it gathers force and widens the breach between people.

“Therefore stop contention before a quarrel starts.”

“Therefore” draws the practical lesson. The time to stop strife is at the beginning, when a quiet word or a decision to drop the matter can still end it. To “stop contention” is to leave it, to walk away from the dispute before “a quarrel starts” and breaks out into open conflict. Letting a matter go at that point takes wisdom and humility, and it is far easier than trying to hold back the flood later. This saying opens a group of verses on strife, justice, and friendship, and the cluster closes with another word on strife at 17:19.
14.notes: Where the NKJV reads “before a quarrel starts,” the ESV, NASB, the 1984 NIV and NLT all speak of the dispute before it “breaks out,” which keeps the picture of water bursting through.

15.brief: The LORD finds both kinds of injustice detestable, declaring the guilty innocent and condemning the innocent. Twisting a verdict in either direction offends the righteous Judge, which is why the gospel shows God justifying sinners only through Christ, so that He remains “just and the justifier” (Romans 3:26).
15.explain:
“He who justifies the wicked,”

To “justify” is a courtroom word. It means to declare someone in the right, to acquit him. Justifying the wicked means declaring a guilty person innocent and letting him go free when the evidence condemns him. A judge might do it for a bribe, for friendship, or out of fear. The LORD described His own justice in exactly these terms: “For I will not justify the wicked” (Exodus 23:7).

“and he who condemns the just,”

The opposite error is condemning the just, declaring an innocent person guilty and punishing him. One wrong lets the guilty loose on others; the other crushes the innocent. People tend to excuse one of these, depending on whom they favor. The verse puts both in the same sentence.

“Both of them alike are an abomination to the LORD.”

“Both of them alike” refuses to rank them. Each is “an abomination to the LORD,” something He finds detestable, because each turns truth upside down in the place where truth matters most. The saying applies first to judges, but it reaches anyone who must decide between people. It also raises a question the gospel answers. Paul says God “justifies the ungodly” (Romans 4:5), and He does so without breaking this proverb. In Christ the righteous One bore the condemnation sinners deserved, so that God remains “just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26). The proverb itself speaks of human judgment, but the wider message of Scripture shows why mercy through the cross never bends justice.
15.notes:
The law describes the judge’s task with the same pair of verbs used the right way round: “they justify the righteous and condemn the wicked” (Deuteronomy 25:1).

Isaiah links this injustice to bribery, the subject of 17:8 and 17:23: “Who justify the wicked for a bribe” (Isaiah 5:23).

16.brief: The fool holds money in his hand as if he could buy wisdom, but the purchase is pointless because he has no heart for it. Wisdom cannot be bought like goods at the market; it requires a real desire to learn, and that is exactly what the fool lacks.
16.explain:
“Why is there in the hand of a fool the purchase price of wisdom,”

The verse is a question with a note of irony. The fool holds “the purchase price of wisdom” in his hand. He has money and opportunity, the means to sit under teachers and learn. Proverbs itself uses buying language for wisdom: “Buy the truth, and do not sell it, Also wisdom and instruction and understanding” (23:23). The fool may even imagine that wisdom can be purchased like goods in the market. The question asks what good his money will do him.

“Since he has no heart for it?”

Here is the answer. The fool has “no heart” for wisdom. In Proverbs the heart is the center of thought, desire, and will, and wisdom must be wanted before it can be gained. Money, schooling, and opportunity cannot put wisdom into a heart that does not want it. The fool’s lack is moral, a matter of desire and will, and the saying is not about intelligence. What he holds in his hand is useless because nothing in him reaches for what it could buy.

17.brief: A true friend keeps on loving in every season, and a brother shows what he was born for when hard times come. Together the two lines describe loyal love that does not depend on good circumstances and proves itself most clearly in adversity.
17.explain:
“A friend loves at all times,”

The friend here is a chosen companion, someone close by choice. His love is constant, “at all times,” in prosperity and trouble, when his friend succeeds and when he fails. Love that comes and goes with circumstances is not what this proverb calls friendship. After the warning in 17:9 about how friends are separated, this saying shows what friendship looks like when it holds.

“And a brother is born for adversity.”

A “brother” is family, bound by birth. The line says he “is born for adversity,” as if hard times reveal what a brother is for. The two lines most likely build on each other: the friend who loves at all times proves himself a brother when trouble comes, and a true brother shows his worth in the hard day. Some read the lines as a contrast between steady friendship and kinship that appears only in a crisis, but either way the verse describes loyal love that does not depend on good circumstances. The very next saying, 17:18, adds a needed balance, and Proverbs returns to the friend in 18:24.
17.notes: The NLT renders the second line “a brother is born to help in time of need,” reading it as a statement of what a brother is for.

18.brief: Yet love still needs wisdom: a man lacking understanding strikes hands in a pledge and becomes surety for his friend’s debt. Set right after verse 17, the saying shows that faithful friendship does not call for rash promises that can ruin both friends (compare 6:1–5).
18.explain:
“A man devoid of understanding shakes hands in a pledge,”

This man lacks sense. He “shakes hands in a pledge,” the public gesture that sealed an agreement. Here it seals a promise to stand behind someone else’s debt. The handshake takes a moment, but the obligation can be long and heavy.

“And becomes surety for his friend.”

To become “surety” was to guarantee another person’s loan, promising to pay if he could not. If the borrower failed, the guarantor’s own goods were at risk: “If you have nothing with which to pay, Why should he take away your bed from under you?” (22:27). Proverbs warns repeatedly against such rash pledges, at 6:1–5 and 11:15. Those warnings concern hasty commitments of this kind, not every act of help. The placement of this saying is the point. Coming right after “A friend loves at all times” (17:17), it shows that love still needs wisdom. Loyalty to a friend does not require a promise that could ruin both men. A wise friend may give what he is able and willing to lose, but he does not bind his household to a debt he cannot carry.
18.notes:
The Hebrew phrase behind “devoid of understanding” reads literally ‘lacking heart.’ In Proverbs the heart is the center of thought and judgment, so a man “lacking heart” is one without sense. The KJV margin notes that “understanding” is literally ‘heart,’ and the YLT renders the phrase ‘A man lacking heart.’ The wording recalls the fool of 17:16, who has “no heart” for wisdom.

Where the NKJV reads “for his friend,” the KJV, ESV, NASB and AMP read that he becomes surety ‘in the presence of’ his friend or neighbor, picturing a pledge made publicly before witnesses.

19.brief: Loving transgression and loving strife go together, because sin breeds quarrels. The man who exalts his gate, building his doorway high as a proud display of himself, is courting his own downfall; with verse 14, this saying frames a cluster on strife.
19.explain:
“He who loves transgression loves strife,”

The verb “loves” appears twice. This is not someone who stumbles into an argument. He enjoys conflict, and his love of strife is tied to his love of sin. Transgression and strife feed each other: sin breaks trust and sparks quarrels, and quarrels breed more sin. The line suggests that a settled appetite for conflict usually has sin underneath it.

“And he who exalts his gate seeks destruction.”

The man who “exalts his gate” builds his doorway high, making his house an imposing display of status. Such a man thinks he is seeking honor, but the verse says he “seeks destruction.” Pride invites the downfall it never expects, as an earlier saying put it: “Pride goes before destruction” (16:18). The two lines belong together, because pride is a common source of quarrels: “By pride comes nothing but strife” (13:10). With 17:14, this verse frames the chapter’s cluster on strife, and the lover of strife and the self-exalting man turn out to be close relatives.
19.notes: The Hebrew word behind “gate” means a doorway or entrance. Some interpreters have taken it as a picture of the mouth, so that the man exalts himself by boastful speech. The medieval Jewish commentators Rashi and Ibn Ezra read it this way, and some modern scholars have drawn the same conclusion from Micah 7:5, where Scripture speaks of “the doors of your mouth” (Micah 7:5). That reading is possible but uncertain. Most versions keep the literal image of a door or gate built high, and the warning against pride stands on either reading.

20.brief: Whoever has a crooked heart finds no good, and a twisted tongue falls into trouble. Deceit within and perverse speech without lead to the same end, as the one who schemes and speaks falsely is caught in the very evil he deals in.
20.explain:
“He who has a deceitful heart finds no good,”

A “deceitful heart” is a crooked, twisted heart, one that bends the truth and schemes. Such a person uses deceit to get some advantage, yet he “finds no good.” His schemes do not deliver what he wanted. The crooked way never arrives at the good it promises.

“And he who has a perverse tongue falls into evil.”

The second line moves from the heart to the tongue. A “perverse tongue” turns and twists words, saying one thing and meaning another. Such a person “falls into evil,” tumbling into the very trouble he has been dealing in. The two lines move from the inside to the outside: a crooked heart produces twisted speech, and both end the same way. Deceit sets traps that catch the one who sets them.
20.notes: The Hebrew word behind “evil” can mean harm or calamity as well as moral wrong, so the line pictures the perverse speaker falling into trouble of his own making.

21.brief: The man who fathers a scoffer does so to his sorrow, and the father of a fool has no joy. The saying gives voice to the real grief of parents whose child turns from wisdom; it speaks of their pain, not their blame.
21.explain:
“He who begets a scoffer does so to his sorrow,”

The verse speaks of a father whose child has turned from wisdom. “Begets” ties the sorrow to the bond of fatherhood itself, a bond that cannot be undone. A father cannot stop being this child’s father, and so he cannot stop being hurt by his child’s choices. The NKJV’s “scoffer” names the son as one who holds wisdom in contempt.

“And the father of a fool has no joy.”

The second line states the same grief more starkly: “no joy.” The gladness a father hopes to find in his children is missing. Earlier, 17:6 said the glory of children is their father; here the flow of honor and joy is broken. The proverb gives honest words to a real grief. It describes the father’s pain and assigns him no blame, and it does not say that he caused his child’s folly. Many godly parents have watched a child turn from wisdom, and this saying stands with them in their sorrow. Later, 17:25 adds the mother’s grief.
21.notes: The Hebrew word behind “scoffer” in this verse is kesil, the word normally rendered “fool” in Proverbs, and the ESV, NASB, the 1984 NIV and KJV all read “fool.” The second line uses nabal, the coarse fool of 17:7.

22.brief: Like medicine, a cheerful heart does good to the whole person, while a crushed spirit dries up the bones. Joy and grief reach the body as well as the soul, though the saying is no rebuke to the sick or the depressed and no substitute for medical care.
22.explain:
“A merry heart does good, like medicine,”

A “merry heart” is a glad, joyful inner life. It “does good, like medicine,” bringing health and strength that reach the body as well as the soul. Proverbs treats a person as a whole; what happens in the heart does not stay there. An earlier saying makes the same connection on the outside: “A merry heart makes a cheerful countenance” (15:13). The joy in view is a real gladness of heart, not a forced smile, and it is a genuine good for the whole person.

“But a broken spirit dries the bones.”

A “broken spirit” is a crushed, beaten-down inner life, heavy with grief or despair. It “dries the bones.” In Proverbs the bones stand for a person’s strength and vigor, as in the promise that wisdom will be “strength to your bones” (3:8). Dry bones picture strength drained away. Grief and despair wear down the body as well as the soul, and the proverb observes this honestly. It does not rebuke anyone who is sick or depressed. It does not suggest that a broken spirit can simply be cheered away, and it offers no substitute for medical care. It recognizes that the inner life matters for the whole person, and that a broken spirit needs care, not blame.
22.notes: The NKJV and KJV supply “like” before “medicine,” while the ESV, NASB and the 1984 NIV read ‘is good medicine.’ The KJV margin offers “to” as an alternative, and the YLT reads ‘doth good to the body,’ showing that the short Hebrew line can be construed in more than one way. The point, that joy does real good, is the same in each.

23.brief: Now the bribe is named for what it is: a wicked man takes a gift secretly, behind the back, to bend the course of justice. Hidden payment corrupts judgment, and the secrecy itself shows that he knows the act is wrong (compare Exodus 23:8).
23.explain:
“A wicked man accepts a bribe behind the back”

Now the bribe is named plainly, from the side of the one who takes it. “A wicked man accepts a bribe,” and he takes it “behind the back,” in secret. The picture is of money slipped from the fold of a garment, where a payment could pass unseen. The secrecy is telling. He knows the act is wrong, and honest payments do not need to be hidden.

“To pervert the ways of justice.”

The last line gives the purpose. The bribe is paid “To pervert the ways of justice,” to bend the course of a case or decision away from what is right. The law had already warned that “a bribe blinds the discerning and perverts the words of the righteous” (Exodus 23:8). This saying completes 17:8. There the briber saw his gift as a lucky stone; here the same word shows what the gift actually does. Samuel’s sons were remembered for exactly this sin, for they “took bribes, and perverted justice” (1 Samuel 8:3), and their corruption helped turn Israel toward asking for a king.
23.notes: The Hebrew behind “behind the back” is literally ‘from the bosom,’ the fold of the robe above the belt. The NASB keeps that wording, and the KJV reads ‘out of the bosom.’ Proverbs uses the same picture of a secret payment in 21:14: “a bribe behind the back” (21:14).

24.brief: The person of understanding keeps wisdom right in front of him, in clear view and within reach. The fool’s eyes wander to the ends of the earth, always looking somewhere else, so the wisdom close at hand goes unseen.
24.explain:
“Wisdom is in the sight of him who has understanding,”

The person of understanding keeps wisdom “in the sight,” right before his face. He does not need to search far for it. It is near, and he keeps it in view, attending to the duty at hand, the counsel he has already received, and the next right step. Wisdom for him is practical and present.

“But the eyes of a fool are on the ends of the earth.”

The fool’s eyes wander. They are “on the ends of the earth,” gazing at far horizons, always looking somewhere other than where wisdom is. He dreams of what is distant and misses what is near. The contrast is between focus and distraction. The fool may imagine that wisdom lies somewhere exotic or far away, but his real trouble is that he will not look at what is in front of him. With 17:16, where the fool holds the price of wisdom yet has no heart for it, this saying shows the same problem from another angle: what he needs is within reach, and his attention is elsewhere.

25.brief: A foolish son brings grief to his father and bitterness to the mother who bore him. Returning to the theme of verse 21, this saying adds the mother’s pain, showing that a child’s folly wounds both parents.
25.explain:
“A foolish son is a grief to his father,”

The Hebrew word behind “grief” carries vexation as well as sorrow, the heartache and provocation a son’s folly causes. The line echoes 17:21 and the opening of Solomon’s proverbs: “A wise son makes a glad father, But a foolish son is the grief of his mother” (10:1).

“And bitterness to her who bore him.”

The second line names the mother, and it names her in a way that reaches back to the child’s birth: “her who bore him.” The one who carried him and brought him into the world now tastes “bitterness” because of the way he lives. A mother’s pain over a wayward child is real and deep, and Scripture honors it. Where 17:21 spoke of the father, this verse makes clear that a child’s folly wounds both parents. As before, the saying voices their grief without blaming them for their son’s choices.

26.brief: Punishing the righteous is wrong, and striking noble men for their uprightness is wrong as well. Following the bribe of verse 23, the saying continues the protest against twisted justice, this time aimed at those who penalize integrity.
26.explain:
“Also, to punish the righteous is not good,”

“Also” adds this saying to the chapter’s list of injustices, following the bribe of 17:23. To “punish the righteous” is to penalize someone who has done right. The verse calls it “not good,” a mild understatement that leaves the reader to feel its weight. Penalizing the righteous turns justice upside down, as 17:15 has already said.

“Nor to strike princes for their uprightness.”

“Princes” are nobles, people of rank and character, the same word used in 17:7. To “strike” them is to flog or beat them, and the shocking part is the reason: “for their uprightness.” They are punished because they did right. Integrity itself has become the charge against them. A court or ruler that does this has inverted justice. The verse joins 17:15 and 17:23 in the chapter’s protest against twisted judgment, and it adds the special wrong of treating uprightness as an offense.
26.notes: The Hebrew verb behind “punish” is anash, which most often means to impose a fine, and the ESV, NASB, AMP and YLT read “fine” here. The same verb appears in the law’s penalty for injuring a pregnant woman: “he shall surely be punished accordingly as the woman’s husband imposes on him” (Exodus 21:22). If a fine is in view, the verse moves from a lesser penalty in the first line to a beating in the second, and both are unjust because they fall on the righteous.

27.brief: The person who has knowledge holds back his words, and the man of understanding keeps a calm spirit. Restraint in speech and a cool temper belong together as marks of real understanding.
27.explain:
“He who has knowledge spares his words,”

To “spare” words is to hold them back and use them sparingly. The person who really knows does not need to say everything he knows or answer every remark. Restraint in speech is a mark of knowledge, because the one who understands a matter weighs his words, while the one who speaks freely often reveals how little he knows. Proverbs said the same earlier: “he who restrains his lips is wise” (10:19).

“And a man of understanding is of a calm spirit.”

A “calm spirit” is a cool, steady temper. The man of understanding does not boil over; when others grow heated, he stays settled. The two lines belong together. A hot spirit spills words, and a cool spirit can hold them back, so restraint of the tongue and control of temper are two sides of the same understanding. The calm described here is not coldness or indifference. It is steadiness under pressure, the self-control Proverbs praises in “he who rules his spirit” (16:32).
27.notes: The KJV reads that he is of an “excellent spirit,” with a margin reading “a cool.” The difference comes from the Hebrew text itself. The written consonants are read as qar, meaning cool, while the reading noted in the margin of the Hebrew manuscripts is yeqar, meaning precious or excellent. The KJV follows the marginal reading. The NKJV, ESV, NASB and AMP follow the written text, which suits the parallel with restrained words.

28.brief: Even a fool is thought wise as long as he stays silent, and counted perceptive when he keeps his lips shut. The chapter closes with a touch of irony: silence can hide a fool’s folly for a while, which shows how much wisdom there is in a closed mouth.
28.explain:
“Even a fool is counted wise when he holds his peace;”

The chapter ends with a touch of humor. “Even a fool,” the kind of person the chapter has warned about again and again, “is counted wise” as long as he keeps quiet. People cannot see his folly until he speaks. Silence hides what speech would reveal.

“When he shuts his lips, he is considered perceptive.”

The second line repeats the point: shut lips earn a reputation for perception. The verbs “counted” and “considered” matter. Silence does not make the fool wise; it only makes others think he is. Yet the irony carries a serious lesson that ties the chapter’s close together with 17:27. If silence can cover even a fool’s folly for a while, restraint in speech is clearly part of real wisdom. A closed mouth also makes room to listen, and listening is where learning begins.
28.notes: Job said nearly the same thing to his talkative friends: “Oh, that you would be silent, And it would be your wisdom!” (Job 13:5).
